newsitem.title: USA: U.S. ethanol tax break seen likely to end in 2000.
newsitem.headline: U.S. ethanol tax break seen likely to end in 2000.

text.p: A tax break that helps make ethanol a competitive fuel in the United States is unlikely to be extended when the current legislation expires at the end of 1999, Dennis Hastert (R-IL), deputy majority whip of the U.S. House of Representatives, said on Wednesday.
"After the year 2000 we are going to have to go on our own, that's what my perception is," Hastert said in a televised address from Washington to the Renewable Fuels Association conference here.
Illinois, the number two corn-producing state, is home to Archer Daniels Midland, the leading ethanol producer.
Hastert said the cost-cutting climate in Washington makes it unlikely the federal subsidy, a 5.4 cent per gallon excise tax exemption, will be extended.
Over the next three years, Hastert said, the ethanol industry must promote ethanol to ensure it survives.

Hastert's comments come on the heels of a bill, HR 161, introduced in the House last month by Rep. Philip English (R-PA) which would end tax breaks for large ethanol producers after 1998. The bill defines large producers of ethanol as those with gross annual sales of more than $1 million.

Ralph Groschen, senior marketing specialist at the Minnesota Department of Agriculture attending the conference, said loss of the tax credit could be damaging to recently built ethanol plants in the Midwest.
Minnesota, with eight ethanol plants and three more under construction, leads the nation in ethanol production and is expected to produce 100 million gallons in 1997.
But most of the state's plants were built in the last 3 or 4 years, Groschen said.
"I can't see them continuing, Groschen said. "They need some time to amortize that debt," Groschen said. (c) Reuters Limited 1997
